name: Nora Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the children's ward at the regional hospital, about forty minutes from our town. We get babies with bronchiolitis, which is a chest infection, kids with asthma, broken arms, appendix operations. A day shift is lots of obs, weighing children for doses, calming parents and a lot of bubbles and stickers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the kids, and I love it when a parent finally sleeps because they trust you. What wears me out is the doses, honestly. Children's drugs are all worked out by weight, I'm still slow at it, and I always ask Grace, the senior nurse, to double-check me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a little disappointed. I like the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a useful helper and leave it there. At work I'd still show people the tricks I use, like getting the AI to quiz me on weight-based doses. Online I'd share a few tips, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's fine for my job. I use AI every day for my sister's catering orders and my drug revision. A plateau just means it stays a good helper and nothing more. The real worry is money: Idris and I have less than a month saved and we want to start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and get faster at the doses with daily practice. I'd keep helping my sister's catering business at weekends, doing her orders and invoices with AI for a bit of cash. And we'd try to save two hundred a month for the baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about money, hopeful about the rest. Normal life, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the catering work bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a hundred and fifty a month, sometimes more around weddings and Eid. It's not much, but it's ours. My sister says I've halved her paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make it hard to save two hundred a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Idris's van breaks down, or his hours get cut in the quiet months after Christmas. Then we'd be back to saving nothing. My parents would help, but I'd rather manage ourselves first.

I'd share **tips**, like getting AI to quiz me on **doses**.
think: My **job is fine**, and AI stays a good helper.
Our real worry is **money**: less than a month saved and a **family** planned.
do: Keep doing my sister's **catering orders** at weekends for cash.
Save **two hundred a month** for a baby.

Plans for a **baby** shape her money worries.

Save two hundred a month towards a first baby

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more like it. I think that's the likely one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance, if you're willing to learn. At work I'd volunteer to help bring in the new systems. Online I'd say people should stop waiting for the government and start learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the charting and care plans change, and the dose checks probably get done by AI, which would help me a lot. A computer can write a care plan for a child with asthma. A computer can't make a frightened six-year-old take a nebuliser. So I think I'm fine, and Idris is the one to watch, because delivery routes are all planned by computer already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to be the ward's go-to person for the new AI charting. I'd push Idris to look at an electrician apprenticeship, because it's hands-on and skilled. And I'd grow the catering work, using AI to take bookings, so we have a second income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good. A little uneasy for Idris.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Idris feel about an apprenticeship at his age?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's twenty-nine, so he'd grumble about being the oldest apprentice. But his cousin did it and now earns more than either of us. I'd make him a proper packed lunch every day, that's my deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said stop waiting for the government. Do you think it should help at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Help with apprenticeships and training, yes. Not paying people to sit at home. My dad worked two jobs when we arrived, and that's how I was raised.

say: This kind of change is a **chance** for anyone who's willing to learn.
People should stop waiting for **government** and start **learning**.
think: AI dose checks would **help me**, and children still need a **person**.
Idris's **delivery job** is the one to watch.
do: Offer to be the ward's **go-to person** for AI charting.
Grow the **catering bookings** with AI as a second income.

fieldNote: She sees **opportunity**, and wants to lead on new systems.

Her family's **work ethic** shapes her view of government help.

steps.text: Volunteer as the children's ward lead for AI charting
Help Idris apply for an electrician apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's fast. That would change our plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so get ready, and I'd help anyone on the ward who wanted to learn. Online I'd say families need to pull together now. I'd still be positive, but I wouldn't pretend it's easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the thinking side of nursing goes by 2028: doses, plans, scores, maybe even triage. The hands-on part with children lasts until the robots, around 2031, and I'm junior. My husband drives a delivery van, and I'm a junior nurse with three weeks of savings. AGI by 2028 means we put off having a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn every new system the hospital brings in from day one, and ask for the paediatric high-dependency course so I'm the nurse they can't do without. Idris would start the apprenticeship straight away. We'd postpone the baby for two years and put every spare penny in savings, and lean on my parents if Idris's van work dried up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared of the technology, scared for our plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about putting off the baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad, honestly. My mum keeps asking. But I'd rather have a baby in a stable house than in a panic, and I think God would understand that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year robot gap help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me three years where my hands matter more than my head. I'd use them to become senior enough that I'm the one supervising. Children's nursing needs a person in the room longer than most, I think.

say: AGI is coming fast, so **get ready**, and I'd help any colleague who wants to learn.
think: The **thinking side** of nursing goes by 2028; hands-on lasts until 2031.
Idris's **van job** and our thin savings mean postponing a **baby**.

fieldNote: Her **adaptability** shows: she'd learn first and fastest.

steps.text: Learn each new hospital AI system from its first day

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Good. That's enough to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare and nobody has an excuse. At work I'd run little sessions on the new tools for anyone who wanted them. I'd tell my friends to learn a skill now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm quite sure of this. Five years is enough to become the nurse who can use every new tool and still calm a screaming toddler. That nurse will always have work. I'd be thirty-two with AGI, thirty-five with robots, and I plan to be senior by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the high-dependency course in year two and learn the AI tools as they arrive. Idris would start the apprenticeship next autumn. And we'd try for the baby in a year or two, once Idris is on apprentice pay and we've got two months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, about money. But mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the catering business look like in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister and I would put an AI booking system on it and maybe take on a second kitchen day. It could be real money by 2031. I'd do it alongside nursing, not instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone on the ward you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace, a little. Grace is brilliant but hates computers. I'd make sure to sit with her and show her, because the ward needs her head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's very manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and I'd encourage everyone to learn now while there's no pressure. At work I'd be the one showing people. I'd post the occasional how-to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel good about it. With ten years, I'd stop thinking of AI as a threat and start thinking of it as staff for my sister's kitchen. I'd be thirty-seven and forty, with lots of experience by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep on at the children's ward and get experienced. I'd put what savings we can spare into my sister's catering business as a small partner, maybe five hundred to start. And we'd have the baby in the next couple of years, as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Our money's still tight, but there's time to fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting five hundred into a business when you have under a month saved, is that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is a bit. But it's my sister, and I see the order book every weekend. I'd only do it once we had one month saved first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Idris in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough for him to finish an apprenticeship and qualify. Then he's safer than me, probably. Robots need wiring too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would mean putting off our baby and Idris losing the van work at the same time. What would help is paid apprenticeships for people like Idris and paid time for nurses to do specialist courses. And family, honestly, my parents and my sister are our real safety net.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. God gave me two good hands and a quick head. I'd rather learn the new machines than spend ten years complaining about them. That's how I was raised.

headlineQuote: God gave me two good hands and a quick head. I'd rather learn the new machines than spend ten years complaining about them.
portrait: A **27-year-old** junior nurse on a **children's ward**, still slow at weight-based doses.
She's married to Idris, a **delivery van driver**, with under a month saved and a baby planned.
She uses AI daily, including for her sister's **catering business**, and wants to lead change.
She's **uneasy** about money in most pictures, **anxious** at two years, and **calm** at ten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would mean postponing a **baby** as Idris's van work goes.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for Idris, paid study time for nurses, and **family** support.
